extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of classical mechanics / history of mechanics (advanced undergraduates, graduate students, or interested scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the foundational principles and methods for analyzing equilibrium in statics: Archimedes' axioms for the lever, the notion of statical moment and centre of gravity, and historical deductions (Archimedes, Galileo, Lagrange, Huygens, Stevinus) including the law of the inclined plane and methods of reduction to symmetric/simple cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedes' axiomatic assumptions (lever)
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes starts from the following assumptions, which he regards as self-evident: a. 'Magnitudes of equal weight acting at equal distances (from their point of support) are in equilibrium.' b. 'Magnitudes of equal weight acting at unequal distances (from their point of support) are not in equilibrium, but the one acting at the greater distance sinks.' c. 'Commensurable magnitudes are in equilibrium when they are inversely proportional to their distances (from the point of support).'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes regards these as self-evident but the text stresses that analysis shows experience and many implicit negative/positive observations underlie them. The assumptions serve as the starting point for reducing the general lever problem to symmetric/special cases; care must be taken to recognize hidden experiential content in 'self-evident' axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilibrium determined solely by weights and distances
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim (used as an assumption) that 'the weights and their distances from the supporting point are decisive' in determining disturbance of equilibrium; rest (no motion) is uniquely determined by these determinative conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This assumption is justified by appeal to experience and symmetry (e.g., placing the spectator in the plane of symmetry makes the proposition appear instinctively true). The text warns that such an assumption bundles many implicit experiences and must be critically examined when used as a foundation for further deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction method: reduce general lever cases to symmetric/simple case
rubrics_metrics.description: The analytical method employed by Archimedes and successors: reduce the general proposition of the lever to a particular apparently self-evident symmetric case (e.g., replace a weight by symmetrically arranged pairs of small weights so that symmetry yields equilibrium).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method is praised as explanatory (discovering simpler phenomena within the complicated) but the text also notes philosophical doubts may arise about deriving proportionality solely from the initial symmetric assumption; generalization must be handled carefully and made explicit (as Galileo later did) to avoid hidden assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statical moment principle (P·L)
rubrics_metrics.description: The disturbing effect of a weight P at distance L from the axis of rotation is measured by the product P·L (the so-called statical moment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrine (product P·L) is implicitly introduced by Archimedes and successors when substituting a large weight by many symmetric small weights; without assuming the importance of P·L, several standard deductions (e.g., that a bar suspended by its centre is supported by a weight equal to its own) cannot be proved. The text treats P·L as the kernel of the doctrine of the lever and centre of gravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centre of gravity coordinates and invariance under rotation
rubrics_metrics.description: The coordinates of the centre of gravity of a system of masses are given by weighted averages (e.g., sums like Σ m x / Σ m), and upon rotating the coordinate axes the centre of gravity's coordinates transform accordingly so that the centre remains the same point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the centre of gravity is chosen as the origin, certain sums vanish and remain invariant under rotations; this invariance is used to argue equilibrium properties for different axes and to generalize lever results in a concise mathematical form (as in Lagrange's presentation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Care when inferring equilibrium for all axes from two axes (need for moment proportionality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The text identifies an inference-error: concluding that if equilibrium obtains for two axes in the plane it therefore obtains for every other axis through their intersection; this inference requires that disturbant effects be attributed to weights proportional to their distances from the axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This logical step is nontrivial: one must explicitly assume that the disturbing effect of a weight is proportional to its distance (i.e., adopt the P·L moment model). The passage warns that without this assumption the generalization to every axis is unjustified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation of statical moment notion from wheel-and-axle and pulley considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: By analysing pulleys and the wheel-and-axle, one perceives that the decisive factors are the products of the weights into the perpendiculars let fall from the axis upon the lines of pull; i.e., statical moments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text shows how removing unessential parts of a pulley or representing pulls by tangential rigid radii leads to the same lever-like condition, thereby motivating the general notion of moment from machine geometry (wheel-and-axle analogues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of the inclined plane (Stevinus/Galileo formulations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stevinus' conclusion: 'on inclined planes of equal heights equal weights act in the inverse proportion of the lengths of the planes.' Galileo/Leonardo formulation: equilibrium on an inclined plane satisfies relations such as Q·CB = P·CA (so Q/P = CA/CB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stevinus' chain-on-prism thought experiment is used to avoid the possibility of perpetual motion and to deduce the proportionality law; Galileo derives the law by reducing the inclined plane to an equivalent lever-rotation picture. The text notes Stevinus' argument relies on an instinctive denial of perpetual motion and that experimental factors (friction, etc.) can obscure direct empirical verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of symmetry as justification for equilibrium on certain supports
rubrics_metrics.description: Equilibrium on a horizontal table: because the pressure is directly perpendicular to the plane and by the principle of symmetry, equilibrium subsists; similar appeals to symmetry justify simple Archimedean cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symmetry provides immediate, instinctive justification for equilibrium in many simple arrangements (e.g., equal weights at equal distances). However, the text emphasizes that such instinctive appeals hide underlying experiential content and must be scrutinized when used as the sole justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phenomenon explained when reduced to known simpler phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: The text asserts that 'we regard a phenomenon as explained, when we discover in it known simpler phenomena' — the objective of Archimedes and successors was to discern the simpler in the more complicated (or vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reductionist explanatory standard underlies the methods presented: reducing machines (inclined plane, pulleys, wheel-and-axle) to lever-like arguments. The author also cautions that such reductions can mask hidden assumptions and so require critical inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and limits of instinctive knowledge in mechanical reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Stevinus and others appeal to 'instinctive knowledge' (principles like symmetry or the impossibility of perpetual motion) as starting-points for reasoning; such instinctive cognition often has high logical cogency but is fallible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text recommends investigating the origin and conditions of instinctive knowledge (what experiences underlie it) rather than treating it as infallible. Instinct is valuable in familiar provinces but must be supplemented by explicit principles (e.g., moment proportionality) for rigorous generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of infinitesimal/elemental motion reasoning (Galileo's small-rotation argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: Galileo's method: consider a very slight rotation of a weight attached so that its instantaneous path element coincides with the inclined plane; the instantaneous element of motion suffices to analyze equilibrium and derive the law of the inclined plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This emphasizes using the character of instantaneous (infinitesimal) motion elements to replace complex motion paths for equilibrium analysis; it justifies reasoning about equilibrium from the initial tendency to move rather than full subsequent motion.
